About the role
As Research Associate in AI for Environmental Forecasting (SENTINEL project), you will lead the AI development strand of SENTINEL, a UKRI-funded project developing a physics-informed AI forecasting system for chemical fugitive emissions. You will build a multi-modal training dataset and design, train and evaluate the Receptor Transfer Function Learner, combining generative AI downscaling, graph neural networks and explainable AI to forecast community exposure to fugitive emissions 24 to 72 hours ahead. You will work with real-world environmental, meteorological, operational and community data, applying rigorous, reproducible research methods and using GPU and high-performance computing facilities.
Working within the School of Engineering, you will collaborate with an interdisciplinary team spanning AI, atmospheric dispersion, chemical fate and public health, as well as project partners including the UK Health Security Agency and the Met Office. You will benchmark SENTINEL against established dispersion models, contribute to high-quality research publications and dissemination, and help develop collaborations and future research opportunities. The role sits within a research environment where AI is being applied to complex datasets and global challenges, including environmental monitoring and sustainability.
About you
You will have a PhD, equivalent professional qualification or equivalent experience in computer science, machine learning, data science, environmental data science, physics, engineering or another related quantitative discipline. You will bring demonstrable experience of developing and training machine learning or deep learning models using real-world, noisy or time-series data, alongside strong analytical problem-solving skills and experience contributing to peer-reviewed publications or equivalent research outputs. You will have strong Python programming skills, including experience with modern AI or deep learning tools such as PyTorch, TensorFlow or JAX and scientific Python tools such as NumPy, pandas or xarray.
You will be able to work effectively both independently and as part of a collaborative research team, communicate complex information clearly and engage confidently with internal and external stakeholders. Experience with graph neural networks, generative or diffusion models, physics-informed machine learning, explainable AI, weather or geospatial data, atmospheric dispersion modelling, or training models using GPU clusters or HPC would be advantageous. You will join a research environment in which high-performance AI, physics-informed approaches and digital twins are being developed for applications including environment, health and engineering.
Additional information

Informal enquiries are welcomed and should be directed to Dr Timothy Pearce at tcp1@leicester.ac.uk

About the role
We are looking for a Research Associate with a process engineering background to play a leading role in the University of Leicester’s RECLAIM project, developing short-loop recycling pathways for end-of-life electric vehicle batteries. Working with researchers in the Centre for Sustainable Materials Processing, you will lead the scale-up of Leicester’s oil-water separation technology from kilogram-scale batch experiments towards a continuous modular pilot process, helping advance the technology from laboratory validation towards industrial demonstration. The Centre specialises in translating and scaling up academic research and pilot processes through collaboration with industrial partners, with established research in lithium-ion battery recycling and the circular economy.
You will design, develop and optimise processes for mixed battery-chemistry black mass, including NMC and LFP, establishing mass and energy balances, operating windows and scale-up criteria. You will translate laboratory findings into engineering specifications and support the procurement, construction, commissioning and validation of a pilot unit capable of processing 100 kg of battery black mass per hour. Working closely with research and industrial partners, including at the Widnes demonstration site, you will contribute to technical reporting, publications, intellectual property, dissemination and future funding proposals, while supporting colleagues and students across the wider research programme. Regular travel to partner sites and hands-on pilot trials will form part of the role.
About you
You will have a PhD, or equivalent industrial experience, in chemical engineering, process engineering, mechanical engineering, mineral processing, separation science or a closely related discipline. You will bring experience of process scale-up, particularly translating laboratory or batch processes into pilot-scale or continuous operation, alongside practical experience of the design, specification, procurement, construction, commissioning or validation of pilot equipment. You will also have knowledge of relevant separation processes, such as solid-liquid or liquid-liquid separation, flotation, emulsions, particle separation or hydrometallurgy.
You will be an effective analytical problem-solver who can work independently while contributing positively to a collaborative research environment. Excellent written and verbal communication skills will enable you to explain complex technical information and work effectively with internal and external stakeholders. Experience of battery materials, black mass, critical-mineral recovery, recycling or powder processing would be particularly relevant, as would experience of industrial partnerships, process safety, technical specifications, commissioning documentation or process-performance analysis. The role sits within the University’s interdisciplinary School of Chemical, Earth and Environmental Sciences, whose research includes Sustainable Materials and Resources and combines scientific research with cross-disciplinary collaboration.

 The Faculty of Medicine at the University of Southampton invites applications for a full-time, fixed-term Research Fellow to join Professor Hanieh Yaghootkar’s interdisciplinary precision-diabetes research programme investigating the heterogeneity of obesity and its impact on type 2 diabetes and related complications. Based at University Hospital Southampton, you will investigate why individuals with similar levels of adiposity differ substantially in their risk of developing type 2 diabetes and its complications. Working alongside genetic epidemiologists, clinicians and data scientists, you will apply statistical genetics approaches, including genome-wide association studies (GWAS), Mendelian randomisation and post-GWAS analyses, to identify genetic determinants, investigate causal relationships and uncover biological pathways linking obesity to metabolic disease.

 As a Research Fellow, you will: 

 Investigate the genetic and biological heterogeneity of obesity and its relationships with type 2 diabetes and related complications.

 Conduct genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of obesity-related traits, adiposity phenotypes and metabolic outcomes using large-scale genetic and epidemiological datasets.

 Apply Mendelian randomisation and complementary genetic epidemiological approaches to investigate potential causal relationships between different aspects of adiposity, type 2 diabetes and its complications.

 Perform post-GWAS analyses, including fine-mapping, functional annotation, gene prioritisation and pathway enrichment, to identify genes and biological mechanisms underlying obesity-related metabolic risk.

 Investigate the genetic determinants of different obesity-related phenotypes and their associations with metabolic and cardiometabolic outcomes.

 Contribute to high-quality scientific publications, conference presentations and the dissemination of research findings.

 Collaborate with multidisciplinary researchers across genetic epidemiology, statistical genetics, genomics, clinical medicine and data science.

 You will have opportunities to develop your expertise in statistical genetics and genetic epidemiology, contribute to innovative analytical approaches and build your publication record within an internationally collaborative research environment. 

 You will have: 

 A PhD in genetic epidemiology, statistical genetics, bioinformatics, biostatistics, computational biology or a closely related discipline.

 Experience analysing large-scale genetic, genomic or epidemiological datasets, ideally including UK Biobank.

 Strong computational skills, including proficiency in R and/or Python and experience working in Linux-based computing environments.

 Knowledge of GWAS methodology, including genetic data quality control, association testing and interpretation of results.

 Knowledge of Mendelian randomisation methods, including instrumental variable assumptions, sensitivity analyses and interpretation of findings.

 Knowledge of post-GWAS approaches, such as fine-mapping, functional annotation, gene prioritisation, colocalisation or pathway analyses.

 An understanding of genetic epidemiology and statistical methods used to investigate the genetic architecture and biological mechanisms of complex diseases.

 Evidence of high-quality research outputs, including peer-reviewed publications.

 Excellent analytical, organisational and communication skills, with the ability to work independently and collaboratively within multidisciplinary research teams. 

 Experience in obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiometabolic disease research or the genetic analysis of adiposity-related traits would be advantageous.

 At Southampton, you will join a supportive, internationally connected research environment at the forefront of genetic epidemiology, data science and metabolic disease research. 

 We offer: 

 Access to large-scale genetic and biomedical datasets, high-performance computing infrastructure and secure analytical environments.

 Opportunities to investigate the genetic and biological mechanisms underlying obesity heterogeneity, type 2 diabetes and its complications.

 Collaboration with leading researchers across human genetics, genomics, epidemiology, clinical medicine and computational science.

 Opportunities for high-quality publications, scientific conferences, professional development and career progression.

 A competitive University benefits package, including pension provision and generous annual leave

 For informal enquiries, contact Professor Hanieh Yaghootkar h.yaghootkar@soton.ac.uk

 About the role 

 We are looking for a talented and motivated Research Associate to join the University of Leicester’s Centre for Healthcare Innovation, Policy and Management within the School of Business. You will take responsibility for the design, organisation and delivery of a systematic review exploring the organisational and behavioural enablers of multidisciplinary health systems leadership. Working with Professor Gregory Maniatopoulos and the wider research team, you will develop the review protocol and search strategies, lead literature identification and screening, undertake data collection, analysis and critical appraisal, and synthesise the resulting evidence into high-quality research outputs.

 The Centre provides an interdisciplinary research environment bringing together academics, doctoral researchers and professionals working across healthcare innovation, public policy and implementation. Its research seeks to strengthen the evidence base for improving health and care services, working with regional, national and international partners. In this role, you will work both independently and collaboratively to achieve project milestones, prepare academic papers and research reports, disseminate findings at regional and national events, and contribute to future research and funding opportunities relating to health systems leadership.

 You will have a PhD in health services research, sociology, health psychology or a related discipline, together with significant experience of systematic reviews and evidence synthesis. You will have demonstrated knowledge of systematic review methodology, including protocol development, search strategies, screening, data extraction, quality appraisal and evidence synthesis, alongside experience of qualitative and quantitative data analysis. You will also bring knowledge and understanding of health systems, healthcare organisations or systems leadership, and experience of managing research projects and preparing applied health and care research for publication.

 You will be a strong analytical and critical thinker who can synthesise complex evidence rigorously and work with a high degree of autonomy while contributing effectively to a multidisciplinary research team. Excellent written and verbal communication, organisational and project management skills will enable you to manage competing priorities, meet agreed milestones and communicate complex findings clearly to academic, professional and non-academic audiences. Knowledge of multidisciplinary working or organisational and behavioural approaches to healthcare, experience with systematic review and reference management software, and experience working with healthcare professionals, policymakers or other relevant stakeholders would be advantageous.

Position: Embedded Systems and Instrumentation Engineer (KTP Associate) 

Based at: Vernon Morris, Deeside 

Salary: Up to £41,600, dependent on experience  

The role: 

An exciting opportunity has become available for a graduate to work full time on a 32-month Knowledge Transfer Partnership (KTP) to develop embedded systems engineering expertise to support product innovation within the water sector. 

Employed and supported by an academic team from the University, you will be based at Vernon Morris' premises in Deeside. 

To find out more about Vernon Morris, go to https://vernonmorris.co.uk/

 

Qualifications we require: 

Hold, or be about to obtain, a minimum 2:1 in Electronic Engineering (or equivalent experience/related degree).
Prior industry experience and/or a higher qualification (e.g., MSc, PhD) in Electronics engineering would be beneficial.  

Application requirements:  

Skills: 

Knowledge of embedded electronic circuit systems, electromagnetic flow sensing system, PCB architecture, and battery systems, with experience of relevant software packages (e.g. MATLAB). 
Knowledge of multi-sensor technologies, signal conditioning and data acquisition. 
Data science experience (database creation, data management, analytics, aggregation, and visualisation capabilities) and familiarity with relevant software (e.g. Power BI). 
Product design for industrial applications, with experience of durability, human-centred design, physical ergonomics, and digital interactivity. 
The ability to work independently to resolve technical issues and work collaboratively.  

Experience: 

Industry experience in designing/developing electronic products, including systems and physical housing integration and testing. 
Exposure to good scientific practice and demonstrable ability to lead a technically complex project. 

 

Please note that this role requires your current right to work in the UK to be valid until the end of the contract. If your current right to work is due to expire before the end of the contract, you will be required to apply for an appropriate visa to cover the full duration of the contract, prior to commencing employment. Should you be successful in securing this KTP contract, our UKVI Immigration & Compliance team will be able to advise and support you through the process.

For 50 years, Knowledge Transfer Partnerships (KTPs) have been helping to innovate for growth by connecting businesses that have an innovation idea with the academic expertise to help deliver it. Currently around 800 businesses, 100 knowledge bases and over 800 graduates are involved in KTPs – collaborative, transformative three-way partnerships creating positive impact and driving innovation.

£2,000 per year to spend on personal training 
opportunity to register on a higher degree at a reduced cost 
opportunity of a permanent position with the company: 70% of host companies make a permanent job offer to their Associate at the end of the project 

 

For an informal discussion, please contact Dr Weizhuo Wang w.wang@mmu.ac.uk and Professor Bamidele Adebisi b.adebisi@mmu.ac.uk. 

Apply at https://manmetjobs.mmu.ac.uk/jobs by submitting a CV and a covering letter detailing how you meet the criteria for the role. Only applications with a covering letter will be considered. 

Due to the nature of KTP funding, this opportunity is intended for candidates who have not already completed more than one year on a previous KTP. Applications from those who have may still be considered on a case-by-case basis.

About the role

A Research Associate post is available in the Local Health and Global Profits consortium. This grant is funded by UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) and is one of the four themes within the Population Health Improvement Network. You will be joining a friendly and dynamic team of multidisciplinary researchers working at the cutting edge of public health research on the commercial determinants of health. The role will be based within the Centre for 21st Century Public Health at the University of Bath.

The post holder will deliver applied public health policy research, with a focus on the commercial determinants of health, using qualitative and/or mixed methods, specifically:

About the role

We are seeking a motivated Research Associate to join our research team at the University of Bath, contributing to the ARIA-funded Robot Dexterity Programme. The project aims to advance the fundamental understanding, modelling and control of robotic systems, with a particular focus on developing new analytical and computational frameworks for dexterous soft robotic manipulators. The successful candidate will contribute to ground breaking research at the intersection of computational mechanics, robotics and intelligent modelling, working within a multidisciplinary team to bridge fundamental physical principles and practical robotic applications.

Key responsibilities include:

High-fidelity computational modelling: Develop and validate advanced physics-based models of robotic systems, including nonlinear mechanics, structural dynamics, large deformation and multi physics interactions, using numerical simulation tools such as COMSOL, ABAQUS or ANSYS.

Robotic modelling and dynamics: Investigate the kinematics, dynamics and actuation of robotic manipulators, particularly soft and continuum robots, and establish computational frameworks that capture their complex physical behaviour.

Experimental validation: Design and conduct experiments to validate high-fidelity computational models of robotic systems, integrating experimental measurements with numerical simulations to assess model accuracy, investigate dynamic behaviour and support the development of robotic manipulation and control.

Research collaboration and validation: Work closely with researchers in robotics, modelling and control to validate theoretical developments through simulations and experiments, contribute to scientific publications, and support the delivery of project achievements.

A PhD (or nearing completion) in Mechanical Engineering, Robotics, Computational Mechanics, Applied Mathematics or a closely related STEM field, or equivalent relevant research experience.

A New Science of Death: Microbial Mortality as a Window into the Architecture and Meaning of Life

We invite applications for five postdoctoral research fellowships funded by the Templeton World Charity Foundation in a project entitled “A New Science of Death: Microbial Mortality as a Window into the Architecture and Meaning of Life”.

This project is the first step in our long-term scientific goal of discovering how the ways in which living organisms die have shaped life from its origins to the present day. The project combines experimental science with sustained engagement from scholars in the arts, humanities and social sciences (AHSS), creating a uniquely interdisciplinary framework for understanding death as both a biological process and societal phenomenon.

Project Director Prof Wilson Poon (Edinburgh) and co-Director Prof Cait MacPhee will coordinate a team of scientists – Prof Filippo Menolascina and Dr Aidan Brown (Edinburgh), Prof Teuta Pilizota (Cambridge), Prof Stuart West (Oxford) and Prof Martin Cann (Durham) – to study how microbes die and the fate of the biomolecules that remain in the ecosystems they occupied. Throughout the project, these scientists will engage in an ongoing dialogue with scholars from AHSS, coordinated by Prof Jane Calvert (Edinburgh) and Dr Fred Simmons (Center for Theological Sciences, Princeton) to facilitate a genuine two-way exchange of knowledge, exploring the wider implications of the scientific research while allowing perspectives from the AHSS disciplines to inform the experimental programme.

The fellows will work in five science work packages that examine how stressed cells transition toward death (Cambridge, working with Prof Teuta Pilizota), how dead cells are broken down into nutrients for other living organisms (Durham, working with Prof Martin Cann), how death can shape the architecture of microbial communities (Edinburgh, working with Prof Cait MacPhee and Filippo Menolascina), the evolution of death strategies (Oxford, working with Prof Stuart West) and the energetics of death (Edinburgh, working with Dr Aidan Brown).

The specific requirements for each post are detailed separately, but we expect each appointee to have the aptitude and interest to contribute to other work packages and to show a genuine interest in the wider transdisciplinary explorations. In particular, they will play a full role in three annual workshops exploring the theological, philosophical and sociological dimensions of the emerging science of microbial death.

Working at Durham University  

A globally outstanding centre of teaching and research excellence, a warm and friendly place to work, a unique and historic setting – Durham is a university like no other.

As one of the UK’s leading universities, Durham is an incredible place to define your career. The University is located within a beautiful historic city, home to a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and surrounded by stunning countryside. Our talented scholars and researchers from around the world are tackling global issues and making a difference to people's lives.  

We believe that inspiring our people to do outstanding things at Durham enables Durham people to do outstanding things in the world. Being a part of Durham is about more than just the success of the University, it’s also about contributing to the success of the city, county and community.

Our University Strategy is built on three pillars of research, education and wider student experience, but also on our keen sense of community and of inspiring others to achieve their potential. 

Our Purpose and Values

We want our University to be a place where people can be free to be themselves, no matter what their identity or background. Together, we celebrate difference, value one another and are each responsible for creating an inclusive community that is respectful and fair for all.

Find out more about the benefits of working at the University and what it is like to live and work in the Durham area on our Why Join Us? - Information Page

The Role and Department

Biosciences is one of the very best departments in the UK (2nd Guardian 2027, 4th Complete University Guide 2027) and it has an outstanding reputation for excellence in teaching, research, and the employability of our students. The department provides a dynamic and interdisciplinary research environment, with the Cann group located within bespoke laboratories for interdisciplinary work at the biology-chemistry interface

The Role

Death is ubiquitous in biology and fundamentally important to life. Across ecosystems, nutrients locked within dead organisms are recycled and reused to support the growth of new life. Yet not all nutrients are equally valuable. Some biomolecules can be used immediately, whereas others require substantial processing before they can be assimilated.

This raises a fundamental question: have organisms evolved mechanisms that continue to function after death, transforming cellular material into forms that other organisms can more readily reuse?

Our recent work identified the bacterial Lon protease as one such mechanism, demonstrating that cellular proteins can continue to be degraded after death into fragments readily taken up by neighbouring cells (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-56761-6). We now hypothesise that this phenomenon is widespread and that many bacterial enzymes possess dual functions: roles in the physiology of living cells and previously unrecognised post-mortem activities that promote nutrient recycling.

To test this hypothesis, the successful candidate will combine transcriptomics, metabolomics, genetics and large-scale Escherichia coli mutant collections to identify gene products that function after death and determine how they contribute to nutrient acquisition by living bacteria. The project will combine experimental microbiology with systems-level approaches to uncover the molecular mechanisms linking death to nutrient recycling. The work will provide fundamental insights into how bacterial communities recycle nutrients and how post-mortem biochemical processes shape ecosystem function.

The postdoctoral researcher will be based in the laboratory of Professor Martin Cann in the Department of Biosciences at Durham University and will be part of a major interdisciplinary consortium involving researchers at Durham, Edinburgh, Oxford and Cambridge. Together, the consortium seeks to establish a new understanding of death as an active biological process that shapes ecosystems through nutrient recycling.

Publications from the PI in this and related fields can be found here: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=cann+mj&sort=pubdate&size=200

Working at Durham 

A competitive salary is only one part of the many fantastic benefits you will receive if you join the University:

You’ll receive 30 days annual leave per year in addition to 8 public holidays and 4 customary days per year – a total of 42 days per year. The University closes between Christmas and New Year.

Applications are invited for a fixed term full-time Research Technician position to work on developing stress resilience in rice. The role involves two linked projects, one which seeks to develop Temperature Resistant (TempR) Rice by exploiting novel germplasm to deliver improved heat tolerance and future-proofed rice yields and the other “Validation of root diameter as a key root trait for stress resilience”. The project is based in the laboratories of Prof Zoe Wilson and Erik Murchie (Sutton Bonington Campus, University of Nottingham, UK). 

 

Rice reproduction, especially pollen development and photosynthesis, are extremely sensitive to heat stress, resulting in major impacts to seed set, posing a significant threat to future yield and food security. It is not known whether the failure of reproduction is because pollen development is particularly sensitive to heat, or a secondary consequence of disruption of energy generation by impaired photosynthesis, or a combination of both. This project aims to address this fundamental question, alongside developing rice germplasm and markers to enable rapid trait deployment in breeding programmes for heat stress resilience in an agricultural field environment. The work involves a partnership with the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) in the Philippines, which will enable testing of rice germplasm under in-field conditions of heat stress, and utilisation of their rice populations that have been established for heat resistance and trait identification and deployment. It will also involve detailed analysis of several candidate genes that we have already identified along with their resultant phenotype. 

Applicants must be highly motivated and meticulous, with experience in growing plants, analysing plant physiology, and molecular biology techniques.  Experience in working with rice, plant reproduction, photosynthesis and advanced physiological techniques is desirable. 

This is a full-time, fixed-term post (36.25 hours) and is available immediately on a fixed term contract until 12th October 2028.  

For more information on our lab activities please contact zoe.wilson@nottingham.ac.uk or Erik.Murchie@nottingham.ac.uk.

 About this role 

 We are seeking an outstanding candidate to work in the Process Dynamics group on understanding how impurities and/or additions to liquid metal alloys can be used to control the final microstructure and defects.

 The successful candidate will work on the design and undertaking of real-time in-situ X-ray imaging solidification experiments to investigate the dynamics of crystal formation both using laboratory and synchrotron sources. 

 The work will focus on the investigation of the solidification of steel and development of novel multi-modal imaging methodologies. Post-solidification measurement of key microstructural features using various microscopy and other techniques will also be performed. 

 The post holder will closely collaborate with other scientists and technicians from the group and the other project partners. 

 The post will be for 1.5 year and based in the Department of Materials at its Begbroke Science Park site, 5 miles north of Oxford. 

 The Project 

 The post is funded by UKRI - Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) grant “Artificial Intelligence X-ray Imaging for Sustainable Metal Manufacturing (AIXISuMM)”.

 The overarching vision of AIXISuMM is to enable the development of transformative, efficient and sustainable manufacturing technologies for producing high-quality recycled aluminium alloys and steel from low-grade scrap materials. The project aims to achieve this by advancing the fundamental understanding of solidification processes and developing strategies to engineer solidification microstructures that can tolerate higher levels of impurities. This will be achieved by harnessing the combined capabilities of multimodal X-ray imaging and in-line artificial intelligence (AI) to uncover the underlying science and accelerate technological innovation. The project brings together a multidisciplinary team of researchers, including the Detector Development Group at the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), Loughborough University, and a consortium of industrial partners. 

 About you 

 The appointed person will be an experimental materials scientist or process engineer with experience in X-ray imaging of solidification or related analytical approach and a doctorate (or be near completion) in materials science or a relevant engineering or physical sciences discipline. 

 Hands-on experience in developing and building bespoke experimental rigs and carrying out experiments in a synchrotron environment is required. 

 The appointed person will require programming skills and experience in computer vision techniques, preferably in Python, for the development of semi and fully automatic data analysis algorithms.

Please do not attach any manuscripts, papers, transcripts, mark sheets or certificates as these will not be considered as part of your application.

Senior Research Associate in Molecular Simulations of the Human Skin Barrier
 Apply
The role

We are seeking a talented computational researcher to join the Notman group at the University of Bristol, contributing to a Royal Society-funded research programme investigating the molecular basis of human skin barrier function and permeability.

The skin provides a remarkable barrier to the external environment but also presents a major challenge for the delivery of therapeutic molecules. Understanding how the organisation and dynamics of skin lipids influence barrier properties is essential for developing more effective approaches to topical and transdermal drug delivery.

Our research uses molecular simulation to investigate these processes at the molecular level. You will contribute to advancing our understanding of skin lipid organisation, molecular permeability and the mechanisms by which chemical compounds influence barrier properties.

This position offers opportunities to undertake new research, develop computational methodologies, publish scientific findings and contribute to the development of reproducible simulation and analysis workflows.

The post is fixed-term until 31 August 2027, based at the University of Bristol. Full-time working is anticipated, although part-time and flexible working arrangements, including hybrid working, will be considered at minumim 21 hours/ 0.6 FTE.

What will you be doing?

Designing, performing and analysing molecular dynamics simulations of skin lipid membranes to investigate their structure, dynamics and permeability.
Investigating computational approaches to improve sampling of complex skin lipid systems.
Analysing existing simulation datasets and undertaking further computational investigations to address outstanding research questions.
Preparing and contributing to scientific manuscripts for publication in peer-reviewed journals.
Developing reproducible computational workflows, including Python-based analysis tools, and supporting the organisation and management of research datasets and code repositories.
Assisting with the supervision and training of undergraduate and postgraduate research students in computational methodologies.

You should apply if

You have a PhD or are near completion, or equivalent research experience in an academic, industrial or clinical setting equivalent to a PhD.
You have experience of molecular dynamics simulations using GROMACS or equivalent software.
You have strong Python programming skills and experience using Linux-based high-performance computing facilities.
You have published at least one peer-reviewed research paper and have experience preparing scientific manuscripts.
You have strong analytical and problem-solving skills, can work independently and communicate scientific findings effectively.
You have experience of lipid membrane simulations, enhanced sampling methods, or computational methodology development. Presenting research at national or international conferences would be advantageous.

Additional information

Contract type: Fixed term until 31/08/2027

Work pattern: Full-time/1.0 FTE (part-time and flexible arrangements considered)

Grade: J

Salary: £45,641 - £51,258 per annum (pro rata if part-time)

School/Unit: School of Biochemistry and Biomedical Sciences

This advert will close at 23:59 UK time on Sunday 15 November 2026

Interviews will take place in week commencing 23 November 2026.  

For informal queries please contact: Rebecca Notman (Associate Professor in Biochemistry) rebecca.notman@bristol.ac.uk

Research Fellow in Host Pathogen Interactions

Research Fellow in Host Pathogen Interactions

Are you an ambitious researcher looking for your next challenge? Do you have an established background in host pathogen interactions and genomic screening? Do you want to further your career in one of the UKs leading research intensive Universities?

We have a vacancy for a molecular and cell biologist to study the host-pathogen interactions of a group of viruses known as the bunyaviruses. This appointment is part of an international collaboration involving scientists working in virology, immunology, structural biology, and cutting-edge image analysis. We seek to understand the formation of viral factories by bunyaviruses within host cells at the molecular and atomic level. One specific goal of the project will be to use genome-wide screening and proteomic approaches to define host restriction factors and molecular components essential for the viral life cycle. The work will involve the implementation of genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9, and haploid cell screening followed by mechanistic dissection via imaging and functional manipulation.

You should have a PhD and post doctorial experience, in host pathogen-interactions, genome-wide screening, molecular biology and cell imaging techniques, as well as a proven publication record in high-ranking journals. The successful candidate will join the thriving research environment within the Faculty of Health and Life Sciences, and have the opportunity to use and gain experience of new state-of-the-art research facilities in cell biology, molecular virology and cell imaging.

What we offer in return

•    26 days holiday plus approx.16 Bank Holidays/days that the University is closed by custom (including Christmas) – That’s 42 days a year!

•    Generous pension scheme options plus life assurance.

•    Health and Wellbeing: Discounted staff membership options at The Edge, our state-of-the-art Campus gym, with a pool, sauna, climbing wall, cycle circuit, and sports halls.

•    Personal Development: Access to courses run by our Organisational Development & Professional Learning team.

•    Access to on-site childcare, shopping discounts and travel schemes are also available.

And much more!

Implementation and Community Research Officer (0.5 FTE) - Fixed Term

The School of Education and Social Sciences at Liverpool Hope has a long history of advancing social justice and programmes of transformative change. Our School is built on a proud heritage that dates to 1844. Since then, we have grown into a dynamic centre for educational excellence and impactful research, with a global outlook and a strong commitment to addressing the challenges facing contemporary society. Today, we continue to build on the vision of our founding educators, creating a vibrant academic environment that reaches beyond the classroom to engage with communities locally, nationally, and internationally. Through our teaching, research, and outreach activities, we strive to make a meaningful difference in the world around us.

Implementation and Community Research Officer

12-month fixed-term contract | 0.5 FTE (17.5 hours per week)

Help us transform public services through meaningful community participation and research.

Building on our successes and commitment to creating positive social change, we are seeking an enthusiastic and motivated Implementation and Community Research Officer to play a key role in delivering an innovative approach to improving public services for British Gypsy and Irish Traveller communities in Flintshire.

Funded by Flintshire County Council, this 12-month post will support the first year of implementation of Connect for Change, a whole-system approach designed by Associate Professor Dan Allen to improve the accessibility, responsiveness and equity of public services for British Gypsy and Irish Traveller communities.

Connect for Change brings together communities, public services and partner organisations to identify and address barriers, strengthen relationships and develop more inclusive and responsive ways of working. This is an exciting opportunity to contribute to translating an innovative approach into practical action, ensuring that community experiences and perspectives are central to shaping change.

The postholder will play an important role in supporting the implementation, community engagement and applied research associated with Connect for Change. This will involve building and maintaining trusted relationships with community members, public service professionals and partner organisations, coordinating implementation activities, supporting meaningful community participation, and identifying barriers, opportunities and areas for improvement.

About you

We are looking for someone with the skills, experience and commitment to work collaboratively with diverse communities and organisations, build positive relationships and support the practical implementation and evaluation of an innovative approach to public service improvement in Flintshire.

The successful candidate will be motivated by the opportunity to contribute to greater equity in public services and to ensuring that the voices and experiences of British Gypsy and Irish Traveller communities inform the development and delivery of services. Candidates should demonstrate a profile of skills and experience aligned with the criteria outlined in the Person Specification.

Join us

We recruit nationally and internationally, seeking talented people who share our ambition to build hope for the future and make a positive difference through their work.

If you are passionate about community participation, social justice and improving public services, and have the drive and commitment to help translate the Connect for Change approach into meaningful action, we would be delighted to hear from you.

Working arrangements: 17.5 hours per week (2.5 days), 0.5 FTE.

Contract: 12-month fixed term.

 Applications are invited for a Qualitative Research Assistant to join the Medical Sociology and Health Experiences Research Group (MS&HERG) within the Nuffield Department of Primary Care Health Sciences at the University of Oxford. 

 The post is funded for 21 months, from 1 January 2027, by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Policy Research Unit (PRU) in Reproductive Health. The study aims to explore adolescent reproductive health needs and interventions to address these. The Principal Investigators are Dr Abigail McNiven and Professor Katy Vincent, with the wider PRU led by Professor Jenny Hall and Professor Judith Stephenson at University College London (UCL). 

 The post-holder will work closely with Dr Abigail McNiven and Professor Katy Vincent, a post-doctoral researcher at UCL, and the wider PRU team. They will contribute to all aspects of the research study, including ethics and research governance, study recruitment, data collection, qualitative analysis and reporting. Through qualitative analysis, the post-holder will explore adolescent reproductive health concerns through existing literature, survey data and focus groups. There may be opportunities to contribute to additional PRU projects.

 You will be a qualitative or mixed methods social scientist with a MA or MSc in a relevant Social Science subject (e.g. Sociology, Social Policy, Social Geography), demonstrable experience in qualitative and mixed methods, and who is able to use social science theory-driven approaches to analysis. Previous experience of research in reproductive health and/or with young people and/or with policy would be advantageous. The role requires you to have a high level of communication and writing skills appropriate for different audiences. You should have the ability to work autonomously, while collaborating effectively as part of a multidisciplinary team across institutions. The ability to work sensitively and develop rapport and trust with research participants from different backgrounds is also essential. 

 The successful candidate must be able to start in post no later than January 2027. 

 You will be based in the Nuffield Department of Primary Care Health Sciences, Radcliffe Primary Care Building, Woodstock Road, Oxford, OX2 6GG as your normal place of work. Consideration may be given to some remote working days, where appropriate. We expect data collection to be largely face to face, so the research will involve visits to participants across the UK and the necessary travel and overnight stays to enable this. 

 For further information or to discuss the post, please contact Dr Abigail McNiven ( abigail.mcniven@phc.ox.ac.uk ). 

 Committed to equality and valuing diversity

Please do not attach any manuscripts, papers, transcripts, mark sheets or certificates as these will not be considered as part of your application.

Overview

The Clinical Trials Research Unit section in the Division of Population Health based in the School of Medicine and Population Health is seeking to recruit a Research Assistant in Medical Statistics (Grade 6) or Research Associate in Medical Statistics (Grade 7) who has a passion for statistics (and applied research) and a willingness to share their passion, enthusiasm and knowledge with others. 

You will have good knowledge of applied statistics and clinical trial methodology. You will have good programming skills and experience of working with complex datasets. You will exhibit a “can do” attitude to new activities knowing your strengths and skills whilst being flexible and able to adapt to change.

You will be able to communicate effectively with non-statisticians, and be able to clearly explain complex statistical concepts in lay terms.  About us 

 Our mission is to maximise and advocate for the holistic health of all children, young people and the adults they will become, through world-class research, education and public engagement. The UCL GOS ICH, together with its clinical partner Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children, forms the largest concentration of children’s health research outside North America. GOS ICH holds an Athena SWAN Charter Gold Award. Please only attach relevant documents to your application (qualifications, cover letters, supporting statements) and avoid attaching large files e.g. research papers, thesis, publications etc.

 About the role 

 This is an exciting opportunity to join the NIHR Policy Research Unit for Healthy Weight (HWPRU) as a Research Fellow. Based within the Public Health and Obesity Group at the UCL Great Ormond Street Institute of Child Health, you will work alongside leading researchers, policymakers and partner organ isations to deliver high-impact, policy-relevant research that informs national decision making. You will contribute to a diverse programme of research focused on healthy weight and obesity prevention. Your responsibilities will primarily involve leading and supporting evidence synthesis projects, including systematic reviews, rapid reviews and other policy-focused evidence reviews. Depending on programme priorities, you may also undertake quantitative analyses of large observational, survey and administrative datasets, and contribute to the development of microsimulation models evaluating the health, economic and equity impacts of obesity-related policies and interventions. Working across the HWPRU's network of eight collaborating institutions, you will engage with researchers, policymakers and other stakeholders to ensure research is timely, rigorous and impactful. The salary offered in this role is £47,186 - £53,638 per annum and is funded for 1 year in the first instance. About you We are seeking a highly motivated post-doctoral researcher with expertise in evidence synthesis and quantitative public health research. You will hold a PhD in public health, epidemiology, evidence synthesis, quantitative methods, food policy or a related field, and have experience conducting systematic reviews and quantitative analyses using statistical software such as R, Stata or Python. The successful candidate will possess strong analytical and critical appraisal skills, with the ability to synthesise complex evidence from multiple sources and apply quantitative and regression-based methods to address policy-relevant research questions. You will have excellent organisational skills and be able to manage multiple projects and competing deadlines while maintaining a high standard of accuracy and scientific rigour. We are looking for someone with strong written and verbal communication skills who can clearly communicate research findings to academic, policy an d practice audiences through reports, publications, presentations and policy briefings. A commitment to reproducible and ethical research, clean coding practices and high-quality data management is essential. You will be a collaborative team player who can work effectively with multidisciplinary colleagues, while also demonstrating the initiative, independence and judgement required to lead complex projects in a fast-paced policy research environment.

 About us 

 The Department of Neuromuscular Diseases is a hub for clinical and research excellence across the spectrum of spinal cord and neuromuscular diseases.

 Based within the department the Cortese Laboratory focuses on the discovery and modelling of novel causes of inherited neuropathies and other neurodegenerative diseases, with particular interest in repeat expansion disorders and conditions caused by variations in non-coding DNA. One of the main commitments of the lab is the further elucidation of the mechanism and development of treatment for RFC1 CANVAS.

 About the role 

 This is an exciting opportunity to join the Cortese Laboratory as a Research Fellow, contributing to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for RFC1 CANVAS and related repeat expansion disorders.

 Building on recent findings demonstrating the potential of CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing to restore RFC1 expression and function, you will investigate complementary therapeutic approaches, including gene reprovision, CRISPR-based activation of endogenous RFC1 and small-molecule strategies to increase RFC1 expression. You will also develop engineered cellular models and CRISPR-based reporter systems to identify genetic and pharmacological modifiers of RFC1 expression through targeted and high-throughput screening, with promising candidates validated in patient-derived and isogenic iPSC-derived neurons.

 Working closely with the ARUK UCL Drug Discovery Institute and the Genetic Therapy Accelerator Centre, you will contribute to an innovative translational research programme combining molecular and cellular biology, genome engineering and drug discovery. The role offers considerable scope to develop new experimental approaches, shape the direction of the project and advance potential therapeutic strategies for RFC1 CANVAS.

 The role is available from 01 November 2026 and is funded by an ERC award for one year in the first instance.

 To apply, please upload a current CV, complete the online application form, and use the supporting statement section or upload a cover letter to outline how you meet the essential and desirable criteria for the role. Please do not upload any additional attachments as these will not be considered by the selection panel

 About you 

 You will have a PhD or equivalent in Molecular Biology, Neuroscience, Genetics, Cell Biology or a relevant discipline, with strong background in molecular and cellular biology, and particular expertise in CRISPR genome engineering, molecular cloning and human iPSC models.

 You will also have a good publication track record and be able to independently design, optimise and troubleshoot molecular and cellular experiments, demonstrating scientific rigour, analytical thinking and problem-solving skills. You will have the ability to supervise students and junior researchers effectively and to contribute positively to a collaborative research environment, as well as excellent interpersonal and communication skills, with the ability to work effectively as part of a multidisciplinary team.

 This role meets the eligibility requirements for a skilled worker certificate of sponsorship or a global talent visa under UK Visas and Immigration legislation. Therefore, UCL welcomes applications from international applicants who require a visa.

 What we offer 

 Appointment as Research Fellow is dependent upon having been awarded a PhD; if this is not the case, initial appointment will be as Research Assistant (salary £40,603 - £43,749 per annum) with appointment as Research Fellow being backdated to the date of final submission of the PhD thesis.

About the Role

A Wellcome-funded Research Assistant post to provide technical support in an enthusiastic, well-established lab analysing the fundamental mechanisms of microtubule organisation and intracellular transport. 

 

The post holder will be a member of the Centre for Mechanochemical Cell Biology and Warwick Medical School benefitting from an outstanding scientific environment and access to state-of-the-art research facilities.

 

The main responsibility of the post holder will be the purification of recombinant human proteins expressed in insect or mammalian cells for biochemical assays, quantitative data analysis and general laboratory support.

 

Informal enquiries including a CV should be sent to a.straube@warwick.ac.uk.

 

For details on the experience and skills required, please refer to the job description (link here).

About You

Candidates are expected to have either a university degree in a relevant subject area (natural sciences, biochemistry, biophysics etc.), vocational training as a laboratory technician or equivalent research experience.

 

Applicants should have a track record in protein engineering, expression, purification and characterisation using biophysical and biochemical experiments, as well as in more generic laboratory support and management, including re-ordering and stock control. Excellent proven manual skills and excellent proven record keeping skills and communication skills, including presentations skills are all essential.

About the Department

You will join the laboratory of Professor Anne Straube in the Centre for Mechanochemical Cell Biology (https://mechanochemistry.org). The Straube lab aims to understand how microtubule arrays are organised and control the morphology of cells. In particular, we use live cell imaging, force measurements, quantitative image analysis tools and in vitro reconstitution experiments to understand the function of motor proteins in organising microtubules and transporting cargo.

 

We offer an outstanding environment for discovery science in one of the best universities in the UK. The Centre of Mechanochemical Cell Biology at the University of Warwick seeks to understand the principles of cellular self-organisation with a focus on mechanisms that enable cell duplication, movement and repair. The centre is home to 20 principal investigators with backgrounds in cell biology, computer science and physics. It is housed in the purpose-built Mechanochemical Cell Biology building with state-of-the art imaging facilities.

 

The post holder will also join Warwick Biomedical Sciences (BMS). BMS has a mission to advance world-class discovery science with an interdisciplinary approach to unravel the fundamental mechanisms of physiological and pathological processes, develop pioneering diagnostic and preventive technologies, and deliver ground-breaking treatments for a healthier future for all. Areas of research excellence focus on quantitative cell and developmental biology, host-pathogen interactions and human reproduction.

About the Role

We are looking for a Senior Research Technician to join and help shape a new new research team studying plant cell biology.

Our projects focus on the fundamental processes that allow plant cells to perceive and respond to their environment, and how these differ across other eukaryotes, including marine algae (diatoms). This will provide novel insights into plant-environment interaction and into the evolution of fundamental cell biology processes across the tree of life.

You will carry out experiments that directly contribute to the group’s research outputs and help keep the lab running smoothly. This includes:

Generating and characterising novel transgenic plant lines, and looking after the lab’s plants and diatom cultures
Keeping stocks, inventories and equipment organised so the whole group can work efficiently
Supporting and teaching colleagues and students, sharing your knowledge and skills
Developing new skills, with technical training and career mentoring provided

 

Any requests for further information about the role can be directed to Alex Johnson (alex.j.johnson@warwick.ac.uk).

 

For details on the experience and skills required, please refer to the job description (link here).

About You

We are looking for someone with hands-on experience of growing and maintaining plants in a laboratory, greenhouse or other controlled environment. You should be able to show that you can:

 

Keep plants or cell cultures healthy on a routine basis, keeping accurate records
Work independently on routine tasks, and keep stocks, inventories and your own workload organised
Work well in a team, sharing your knowledge and skills with colleagues and students

 

Experience of molecular biology (for example, cloning, PCR and genotyping), plant transformation, cell culture or microscopy would be an advantage, but full training will be provided.  About the Role 

 Applicants who have previously applied for this role within the last six months, and were unsuccessful, will not be considered to ensure fairness and allow for meaningful development of experience and skills. 

A Wellcome-funded Research Assistant post to provide technical support in an enthusiastic, well-established lab analysing the fundamental mechanisms of microtubule organisation and intracellular transport. 

The post holder will be a member of the Centre for Mechanochemical Cell Biology and Warwick Medical School benefitting from an outstanding scientific environment and access to state-of-the-art research facilities.

The main responsibility of the post holder will be the purification of recombinant human proteins expressed in insect or mammalian cells for biochemical assays, quantitative data analysis and general laboratory support.

Informal enquiries including a CV should be sent to a.straube@warwick.ac.uk .

 For details on the experience and skills required, please refer to the job description ( link here ).

 About You 

Candidates are expected to have either a university degree in a relevant subject area (natural sciences, biochemistry, biophysics etc.), vocational training as a laboratory technician or equivalent research experience.

Applicants should have a track record in protein engineering, expression, purification and characterisation using biophysical and biochemical experiments, as well as in more generic laboratory support and management, including re-ordering and stock control. Excellent proven manual skills and excellent proven record keeping skills and communication skills, including presentations skills are all essential.

 About the Department 

You will join the laboratory of Professor Anne Straube in the Centre for Mechanochemical Cell Biology ( https://mechanochemistry.org ). The Straube lab aims to understand how microtubule arrays are organised and control the morphology of cells. In particular, we use live cell imaging, force measurements, quantitative image analysis tools and in vitro reconstitution experiments to understand the function of motor proteins in organising microtubules and transporting cargo.

We offer an outstanding environment for discovery science in one of the best universities in the UK. The Centre of Mechanochemical Cell Biology at the University of Warwick seeks to understand the principles of cellular self-organisation with a focus on mechanisms that enable cell duplication, movement and repair. The centre is home to 20 principal investigators with backgrounds in cell biology, computer science and physics. It is housed in the purpose-built Mechanochemical Cell Biology building with state-of-the art imaging facilities.

The post holder will also join Warwick Biomedical Sciences (BMS). BMS has a mission to advance world-class discovery science with an interdisciplinary approach to unravel the fundamental mechanisms of physiological and pathological processes, develop pioneering diagnostic and preventive technologies, and deliver ground-breaking treatments for a healthier future for all. Areas of research excellence focus on quantitative cell and developmental biology, host-pathogen interactions and human reproduction.
